direct_answer: Shell states that its remuneration schemes are designed to support delivery of its corporate strategy, including “reducing our operational emissions” and supporting customers to reduce their emissions [Source 1]. The majority of employees participate in an annual bonus scheme, while Executive Directors (and other nominated employees) receive long-term share awards [Source 1]. Shell indicates that remuneration schemes linked to sustainability include “sustainability-linked measures and targets and metrics used in the performance assessment,” as well as “the proportion of variable remuneration dependent on sustainability-related performance,” and that the Remuneration Committee has a role in “approving and updating the Directors’ Remuneration Policy” [Source 1]. Shell also notes that its energy transition performance is measured against climate-related targets and ambition, including those “reflected in the remuneration of senior management and employees,” with targets focused primarily on reducing absolute GHG emissions and its Net Carbon Intensity (NCI) [Source 4].
compliance_rationale: The passages evidence that Shell links remuneration/incentives to sustainability (notably climate) and identifies scheme types (annual bonus; long-term share awards) and governance involvement (REMCO role in approving/updating Directors’ Remuneration Policy) [Source 1], plus the sustainability dimensions used (absolute GHG emissions and NCI) [Source 4]. However, the retrieved passages do not provide the required GOV-3 granular details (e.g., exact proportion of variable pay tied to sustainability, specific targets/thresholds, and explicit approval/update level details beyond REMCO’s role) because those details are referenced to other pages not included in the provided extracts [Source 1].
disclosure_gaps: Key characteristics of the incentive schemes for administrative, management and supervisory body members (beyond high-level scheme types) are not detailed in the retrieved passages (e.g., structure, time horizons/vesting conditions, payout mechanics).

Whether performance is assessed against specific sustainability-related targets/impacts: climate focus is mentioned, but the specific targets (e.g., target levels, timeframes, thresholds) used for remuneration are not provided in the retrieved passages.

How sustainability-related performance metrics are used as benchmarks or embedded in remuneration policies is only described at a high level; the mechanics of how metrics affect outcomes are not included in the retrieved passages.
The proportion of variable remuneration dependent on sustainability-related targets/impacts is referenced as disclosed elsewhere but is not stated in the retrieved passages [Source 1].

The level at which incentive scheme terms are approved and updated is only partially evidenced (REMCO role mentioned); any additional approval/update levels (e.g., Board/shareholder approval) are not specified in the retrieved passages [Source 1].
